title: AI raises entry-level engineering standards to near-senior level
dek: AI tools now handle foundational coding well enough that companies need architects who can weigh design trade-offs; new graduates' baseline skill bar has risen by a tier.
why: For those seeking to understand how AI is reshaping the engineer skill standard, and how AI startups decide between building or buying tools internally. The middle section on course curriculum details is lower information density.
who: Engineers focused on AI-native engineering practices, tech managers, and founders wanting to understand how AI startups decide whether to buy or build internal tools.
skip: The opening section on specific course selection and curriculum week-by-week details has lower information density and can be skipped.

points.h: Principles stabilize: teach methodology, not case studies
points.body: Year one courses broadly survey how AI applies across the software development lifecycle; year two narrows to principle codification—systematic thinking about context engineering, design, and architecture. This shift mirrors AI engineering maturing from wild growth into accumulated best practice. Course syllabi need annual rewriting since last year's hot company may vanish, but underlying principles are now stable enough to teach as methodology rather than case studies.

points.h: AI erases entry-level positions; newcomers must now architect, not just code
points.body: Graduate hiring expectations have risen from entry-level to near-senior competency—not market inflation, but real change driven by AI. Coding agents handle foundational work so well that the place where newcomers most often stumble is now automated. The floor disappeared, not because the ceiling rose. Companies now need architects who can weigh design trade-offs. When basic coding is off the table, entry-level positions as a category cease to exist.

points.h: Real projects restore the mentorship chain through production code review
points.body: Year two's core innovation: students work directly on real open-source projects—million-line production codebases, not simulated exercises—collaborating with maintainers. This solves a critical problem: mentorship. When AI takes over foundational coding, the knowledge transmission between junior and senior engineers that once flowed through "the process of coding" loses its vehicle. Real code review re-anchors that inheritance chain.

points.h: RPI framework preserves human decisions while scaling to production codebases
points.body: The RPI framework (Research-Proposal-Implementation) isn't concept theater—it's a practical tool for million-line repositories. The logic: Research phase maps the codebase context; Proposal phase surfaces multiple approaches for humans to decide between; Implementation phase executes. This design keeps humans in the decision loop while the tool handles genuinely complex real tasks.

points.h: Buy first to learn, build only when you need control
points.body: Monaco's tool philosophy: buy to learn, build to keep. Early on, they tried multiple CodeReview platforms to validate what they needed, then self-built to retain control. They built Monocoder (based on coder.com) and Slack bot Hal because existing SRE tools lacked maturity. CodeReview was the exception—they chose Devin and stayed with it, because it crossed the usability threshold.

points.h: Code generation now faster than human review; triage beats line-by-line audit
points.body: AI can theoretically produce 30+ PRs a day, but human review throughput hasn't scaled proportionally. If review stays traditional line-by-line inspection, reviewers become the hard bottleneck. Mihail sees the middle ground: triage by risk. Some PRs auto-approve; some need human eyes; and even when humans review, it might be spec-level, not character-by-character.

points.h: Risk-based review: scrutinize auth and payments, trust everything else
points.body: Auth, Billing, Data Storage—three zones marked "no casual code", requiring careful design and review. Everywhere else: "generate freely". This tiering matters because AI-generated code's main risk isn't more bugs—usually fewer—but "you don't know what you wrote". When review capacity can't cover everything, deep inspection on high-risk zones and deference elsewhere becomes the pragmatic trade-off.

points.h: Manager of Agents replaces traditional engineer role, orchestrates system health
points.body: Engineering metrics are shifting. Today it's PR merge rates; in two years, Eric thinks that standard will look absurd. He sketches a new role: "Manager of Agents"—not people management, but orchestrating an agent system, requiring understanding of product goals and technical constraints, decision-making across abstraction layers, setting goals, course-correcting. Even inside Anthropic, the product head and engineering head roles haven't merged yet.
